```{r, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)
library(p8105.datasets)
data("weather_df")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 6,
  fig.asp = .6,
  out.width = "90%"
)

theme_set(theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom"))

options(
  ggplot2.continuous.colour = "viridis",
  ggplot2.continuous.fill = "viridis"
)

scale_colour_discrete = scale_colour_viridis_d
scale_fill_discrete = scale_fill_viridis_d

set.seed(1)
```

## Problem 1: U.S. Homicides

Import and clean 

```{r, message= FALSE}
homicide_df = 
  read_csv("data/homicide-data.csv", 
           na = c("", "NA", "Unknown")) |> 
  mutate(
    city_state = str_c(city, state, sep = ", "),
    resolved = as.numeric(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),
    victim_age = as.numeric(victim_age)
  ) |> 
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c(
      "Dallas, TX",
      "Phoenix, AZ",
      "Kansas City, MO",
      "Tulsa, AL"
    ),
    victim_race %in% c("White", "Black")
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    victim_race = fct_relevel(victim_race, "White"),
    victim_sex = fct_relevel(victim_sex, "Female")
  )
```

#### Baltimore Logistic Regression

```{r}
baltimore_glm = 
  homicide_df |> 
  filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD") |> 
  glm(
    resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
    data = _,
    family = binomial()
  )

baltimore_results = 
  baltimore_glm |> 
  broom::tidy(conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |> 
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |> 
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

baltimore_results |> 
  mutate(term = "Male vs. Female") |> 
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    col.names = c(
      "Comparison", "Adjusted OR", 
      "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"
    ),
    caption = "**Table 1:** Adjusted odds ratio for homicide resolution in Baltimore, MD"
  )
```

In Baltimore, the adjusted odds ratio for solving homicides comparing male victims to female victims is `r round(baltimore_results$estimate, 3)` (95% CI: `r round(baltimore_results$conf.low, 3)`–`r round(baltimore_results$conf.high, 3)`). Holding victim age and race constant, the odds of solving a homicide involving a male victim are approximately `r round((1 - baltimore_results$estimate) * 100, 1)`% lower than those involving a female victim. Since the 95% confidence interval does not contain 1, this association is statistically significant at the 0.05 level.

#### Logistic Regression for All Cities

```{r}
city_results_df = 
  homicide_df |> 
  nest(data = -city_state) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(
      data, 
      \(df) glm(
        resolved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
        data = df,
        family = binomial()
      )
    ),
    results = map(
      models,
      \(model) broom::tidy(
        model,
        conf.int = TRUE,
        exponentiate = TRUE
      )
    )
  ) |> 
  select(city_state, results) |> 
  unnest(results) |> 
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |> 
  select(city_state, estimate, conf.low, conf.high)
```

#### Plot for all Cities

```{r city_or_plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=12, out.width="100%"}
city_results_df |> 
  mutate(
    city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, estimate, .desc = TRUE)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = city_state, color = estimate)) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
    width = 0.2,
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(
    breaks = c(0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4),
    labels = c("0.125", "0.25", "0.5", "1", "2", "4")
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(begin = 0.15, end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted Odds Ratios for Homicide Resolution",
    subtitle = "Male vs. female victims, adjusting for age and race",
    x = "Adjusted Odds Ratio (95% CI, log scale)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(
      color = "gray93", linewidth = 0.3
    ),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11)
  )
```

Across the `r nrow(city_results_df)` cities, `r sum(city_results_df$estimate < 1)` have estimated adjusted odds ratios below 1, suggesting that homicides involving male victims generally have lower odds of being solved than those involving female victims, after adjusting for victim age and race.

New York, NY has the lowest estimated odds ratio (`r round(min(city_results_df$estimate), 3)`), while Albuquerque, NM has the highest (`r round(max(city_results_df$estimate), 3)`).

For `r sum(city_results_df$conf.high < 1)` cities, the 95% confidence interval lies entirely below 1, indicating a statistically significant association at the 0.05 level. However, many cities have confidence intervals that include 1, suggesting insufficient evidence of a difference in homicide resolution odds between male and female victims.

The widths of the confidence intervals vary considerably across cities, reflecting differences in the precision of the estimated odds ratios.

## Problem 2: Central Park Weather

Clean

```{r}
weather_clean_df = 
  weather_df |> 
  select(tmax, tmin, prcp) |> 
  drop_na()
```

#### Fit the Regression Model

```{r}
weather_lm = 
  lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = weather_clean_df)

weather_lm |> 
  broom::tidy() |> 
  mutate(
    term = recode(
      term,
      "(Intercept)" = "Intercept",
      "tmin" = "Minimum temperature",
      "prcp" = "Precipitation"
    ),
    p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c(
      "Predictor", "Estimate", "Standard Error",
      "t-statistic", "p-value"
    ),
    caption = "**Table 2:** Linear regression estimates for maximum daily temperature"
  )
```

Minimum temperature is positively associated with maximum daily temperature, while precipitation is negatively associated with maximum daily temperature, holding the other predictor constant. Both associations are statistically significant ($p < 0.001$). The model explains approximately `r round(broom::glance(weather_lm)$r.squared * 100, 1)`% of the observed variation in maximum daily temperature. This fitted model serves as the basis for the subsequent bootstrap analysis.

#### Bootstrapping 5000 samples

```{r}
weather_bootstrap_df = 
  weather_clean_df |> 
  modelr::bootstrap(n = 5000) |> 
  mutate(
    models = map(
      strap,
      \(df) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = df)
    ),
    glance_results = map(models, broom::glance),
    tidy_results = map(models, broom::tidy)
  )
```

##### Extracting $R^2$

```{r}
bootstrap_r2_df = 
  weather_bootstrap_df |> 
  select(.id, glance_results) |> 
  unnest(glance_results) |> 
  select(.id, r.squared)
```

##### Coefficient Ratio

```{r}
bootstrap_ratio_df = 
  weather_bootstrap_df |> 
  select(.id, tidy_results) |> 
  unnest(tidy_results) |> 
  filter(term %in% c("tmin", "prcp")) |> 
  select(.id, term, estimate) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = term,
    values_from = estimate
  ) |> 
  mutate(beta_ratio = tmin / prcp) |> 
  select(.id, beta_ratio)
```

```{r}
bootstrap_results_df = 
  bootstrap_r2_df |> 
  left_join(bootstrap_ratio_df, by = ".id")
```

#### Plotting the bootstrap distributions

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
bootstrap_results_df |> 
  select(r.squared, beta_ratio) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    quantity = recode(
      quantity,
      r.squared = "R-squared",
      beta_ratio = "Coefficient Ratio"
    ),
    quantity = factor(
      quantity,
      levels = c("R-squared", "Coefficient Ratio")
    )
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, fill = quantity)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.15, end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Bootstrap Distributions of Regression Estimates",
    subtitle = "Based on 5,000 bootstrap samples of Central Park weather data",
    x = "Bootstrap Estimate",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The bootstrap distribution of $r^2$ is approximately bell-shaped with slight left skewness, centered around `r round(mean(bootstrap_results_df$r.squared), 3)` with a standard deviation of `r round(sd(bootstrap_results_df$r.squared), 4)`. The narrow distribution suggests that the estimated proportion of variation in maximum temperature explained by the model is relatively stable across bootstrap samples.

In contrast, the bootstrap distribution of $\hat{\beta}_1 / \hat{\beta}_2$ is noticeably left-skewed, with a longer tail toward more negative values. The distribution has a mean of `r round(mean(bootstrap_results_df$beta_ratio), 2)` and a standard deviation of `r round(sd(bootstrap_results_df$beta_ratio), 2)`. This asymmetry supports the use of bootstrap percentile confidence intervals rather than relying on a normal approximation.

#### Confidenece Intervals

```{r}
bootstrap_ci_df = 
  bootstrap_results_df |> 
  select(r.squared, beta_ratio) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "quantity",
    values_to = "estimate"
  ) |> 
  group_by(quantity) |> 
  summarize(
    lower_ci = quantile(estimate, 0.025),
    upper_ci = quantile(estimate, 0.975)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

bootstrap_ci_df |> 
  mutate(
    quantity = recode(
      quantity,
      r.squared = "R-squared",
      beta_ratio = "Coefficient Ratio"
    )
  ) |> 
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 4,
    col.names = c(
      "Quantity", "Lower 95% CI", "Upper 95% CI"
    ),
    caption = "95% percentile confidence intervals based on 5,000 bootstrap samples"
  )
```

The 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for $r^2$ is (`r round(bootstrap_ci_df |> filter(quantity == "r.squared") |> pull(lower_ci), 4)`, `r round(bootstrap_ci_df |> filter(quantity == "r.squared") |> pull(upper_ci), 4)`). This narrow interval suggests that the model consistently explains a high proportion of the variation in maximum daily temperature.

The 95% bootstrap percentile confidence interval for $\hat{\beta}_1 / \hat{\beta}_2$ is (`r round(bootstrap_ci_df |> filter(quantity == "beta_ratio") |> pull(lower_ci), 2)`, `r round(bootstrap_ci_df |> filter(quantity == "beta_ratio") |> pull(upper_ci), 2)`). The interval is entirely negative, consistent with the positive estimated coefficient for minimum temperature and the negative estimated coefficient for precipitation. The asymmetry of the bootstrap distribution illustrates the usefulness of the percentile bootstrap method for inference on nonlinear functions of regression coefficients.

## Problem 3: Baby Birth Weights

Import and Clean

```{r}
birthweight_df = 
  read_csv("data/birthweight.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    babysex = factor(
      babysex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    frace = factor(
      frace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9),
      labels = c("White", "Black", "Asian",
                 "Puerto Rican", "Other", "Unknown")
    ),
    mrace = factor(
      mrace,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 8),
      labels = c("White", "Black", "Asian",
                 "Puerto Rican", "Other")
    ),
    malform = factor(
      malform,
      levels = c(0, 1),
      labels = c("Absent", "Present")
    )
  )

# Check missing values
birthweight_missing_df = 
  birthweight_df |> 
  summarize(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "missing"
  )
#birthweight_missing_df |> 
  #summarize(
    #total_missing = sum(missing),
    #variables_with_missing = sum(missing > 0)
  #) missing values zero
```

The cleaned birth weight dataset contains `r nrow(birthweight_df)` observations and `r ncol(birthweight_df)` variables. The categorical variables for infant sex, maternal race, paternal race, and malformation status were converted to factors with appropriate labels. A missing data assessment identified `r sum(birthweight_missing_df$missing)` missing values across all variables; therefore, no observations needed to be excluded from the regression analysis.

#### Proposed Regression Model

I used a hypothesis-driven approach to develop a multiple linear regression model for birth weight. I included infant head circumference, birth length, gestational age, and sex to account for infant size and development. Maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, weight gain during pregnancy, smoking, and maternal age were included to account for maternal health and prenatal factors that may influence fetal growth.

Parity was excluded from the final model because `r round(mean(birthweight_df$parity == 0) * 100, 2)`% of observations had a parity of zero. This lack of variability resulted in a rank-deficient model during cross-validation, making its coefficient difficult to estimate reliably. The final proposed model includes eight predictors with main effects only.

```{r}
birthweight_lm = 
  lm(
    bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + babysex +
      ppbmi + wtgain + smoken + momage,
    data = birthweight_df
  )
```

Predicted birth weights and residuals

```{r}
birthweight_residuals_df = 
  birthweight_df |> 
  modelr::add_predictions(birthweight_lm) |> 
  modelr::add_residuals(birthweight_lm)
```

#### Plot For My Proposed Model

```{r}
birthweight_residuals_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = pred, y = resid)) +
  geom_point(
    alpha = 0.25,
    size = 1,
    color = viridis::viridis(5)[2]
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray40"
  ) +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "loess",
    se = FALSE,
    color = viridis::viridis(5)[4],
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs. Fitted Birthweight",
    subtitle = "Proposed multiple linear regression model",
    x = "Predicted Birthweight (grams)",
    y = "Residuals (grams)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

The residuals are generally centered around zero for fitted birth weights between 2,000 and 4,000 grams. However, the smoothed trend line shows noticeable curvature at lower fitted values, indicating that the model tends to underestimate birth weight in this range. Several large residuals and changes in residual variability suggest potential violations of the linearity and constant variance assumptions. Additionally, some predicted birth weights are negative, which is biologically implausible. Although the proposed model performs reasonably well for the majority of observations, its predictions are less reliable at the extremes.

#### Alternative Models

Alternative 1:

```{r}
length_gestation_lm = 
  lm(
    bwt ~ blength + gaweeks,
    data = birthweight_df
  )
```

Alternative 2:

```{r}
interaction_lm = 
  lm(
    bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex,
    data = birthweight_df
  )
```

##### Cross-Validation

```{r}
cv_df = 
  modelr::crossv_mc(birthweight_df, n = 100, test = 0.2) |> 
  mutate(
    train = map(train, as_tibble),
    test = map(test, as_tibble)
  )
```

Fit all three 

```{r}
cv_df = 
  cv_df |> 
  mutate(
    proposed_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(
        bwt ~ bhead + blength + gaweeks + babysex +
          ppbmi + wtgain + smoken + momage,
        data = df
      )
    ),
    length_gestation_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(bwt ~ blength + gaweeks, data = df)
    ),
    interaction_mod = map(
      train,
      \(df) lm(bwt ~ bhead * blength * babysex, data = df)
    )
  )
```

Prediction Error

```{r}
cv_df = 
  cv_df |> 
  mutate(
    rmse_proposed = map2_dbl(
      proposed_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    ),
    rmse_length_gestation = map2_dbl(
      length_gestation_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    ),
    rmse_interaction = map2_dbl(
      interaction_mod, test, modelr::rmse
    )
  )
```

#### Plotting the Cross-validated Prediction Errors

```{r}
cv_results_df = 
  cv_df |> 
  select(.id, starts_with("rmse_")) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    - .id,
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "rmse"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    model = recode(
      model,
      rmse_proposed = "Proposed Model",
      rmse_length_gestation = "Length + Gestational Age",
      rmse_interaction = "Interaction Model"
    ),
    model = fct_reorder(model, rmse, .fun = mean)
  )

cv_results_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = rmse, fill = model)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    fill = "white",
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 23,
    size = 3,
    fill = "black"
  ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.15, end = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Cross-Validated Prediction Error by Model",
    subtitle = "100 Monte Carlo splits with 80% training and 20% testing",
    x = NULL,
    y = "RMSE (grams)",
    caption = "Black diamonds indicate mean RMSE."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank()
  )
```

#### Summary Table

```{r}
cv_summary_df = 
  cv_results_df |> 
  group_by(model) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_rmse = mean(rmse),
    median_rmse = median(rmse),
    sd_rmse = sd(rmse),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |> 
  arrange(mean_rmse)

cv_summary_df |> 
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 2,
    col.names = c(
      "Model", "Mean RMSE", "Median RMSE", "SD of RMSE"
    ),
    caption = "**Table 4:** Summary of cross-validated prediction errors (grams)"
  )
```

Across 100 Monte Carlo cross-validation splits, the proposed model had the lowest mean RMSE of `r round(cv_summary_df |> filter(model == "Proposed Model") |> pull(mean_rmse), 2)` grams, followed by the interaction model at `r round(cv_summary_df |> filter(model == "Interaction Model") |> pull(mean_rmse), 2)` grams and the length and gestational age model at `r round(cv_summary_df |> filter(model == "Length + Gestational Age") |> pull(mean_rmse), 2)` grams.

The proposed model also exhibited the lowest variability in prediction error across testing datasets. Although the proposed and interaction models have overlapping RMSE distributions, the proposed model achieved better average predictive performance. The length and gestational age model performed noticeably worse than both alternatives. These results suggest that incorporating maternal characteristics and prenatal factors alongside infant measurements may improve birth weight prediction. Despite the limitations identified in the residual analysis, the proposed model is preferred among the three models considered based on its cross-validated prediction performance.
